subject: math
title: A-Math quadratics: completing the square, discriminant and inequalities

slides.heading: A-Math quadratics: completing the square, discriminant and inequalities
bullets: Quadratics three ways: complete the square, read the discriminant, and solve inequalities on a number line
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we complete the square as area, use the discriminant to decide the roots, solve a quadratic inequality on a number line, and expose the trap of reading no real roots as no solution.

slides.heading: What we will learn
bullets: Complete the square for x^2 + 6x by adding the missing corner 9
Use D = b^2 - 4ac to decide the roots and solve x^2 - 4 > 0 on a number line
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the negative discriminant trap.

slides.heading: One expression, three questions
bullets: x^2 + 6x can be drawn as area - so what is missing to make it a perfect square?
And if a discriminant comes out negative, has the equation really got no answer at all?
slides.notes: Ask the class to vote: what must be added to x^2 + 6x to complete the square? Take two or three answers, then point out that today the picture, the discriminant and the number line each answer a different question.

slides.heading: Three tools for quadratics
bullets: Completing the square rewrites x^2 + 6x as (x + 3)^2 - 9 by adding the missing corner
The discriminant D = b^2 - 4ac decides the roots: positive, zero or negative
For an inequality, find the roots first, then test each region of the number line
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: the area picture completes the square, the sign of D tells the root story, and the roots split the number line into regions to test.

slides.heading: Completing the square, as area
bullets: Take x^2 + 6x as area: an x-by-x square plus two 3-by-x strips, because half of 6 is 3
The missing corner is 3^2 = 9, so x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x+3)^2
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate: watch one strip slide below the square, then the missing three-by-three corner of area 9 slides in to complete the square.

slides.heading: The discriminant decides the roots
bullets: For ax^2 + bx + c, the discriminant is D = b^2 - 4ac
D > 0 gives two real roots, D = 0 gives one repeated root, D < 0 gives no real roots
slides.notes: Follow the parabola as it sinks: above the axis is D negative, touching is D zero, crossing twice is D positive - the sign of D is the whole story.

slides.heading: Quadratic inequalities on a number line
bullets: For x^2 - 4 > 0 the roots are x = -2 and x = 2, splitting the line into three regions
Testing each region gives the solution x < -2 or x > 2
slides.notes: Watch the test probe travel the number line: x = -3 passes, x = 0 fails, x = 3 passes, so the two outer regions light up as the solution.

slides.heading: A common mistake: a negative discriminant means no solution
bullets: For x^2 + 1 = 0, D = -4, so there are no real roots
The trap claim is: A negative discriminant means the equation has no solution.
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: no real roots is not no solution - the equation x^2 + 1 = 0 still has the two complex roots x = +/-i.

slides.heading: Worked example: completing the square
bullets: Step 1: halve the coefficient of x: half of 6 is 3, and the missing corner is 3^2 = 9
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly: split 6x into two 3x strips, slide one below, and the corner that completes the square is 3 squared, which is 9.

slides.heading: Your turn: quadratics, then check the trap
bullets: Complete the square for x^2 + 6x and solve x^2 - 4 > 0 on a number line
Careful - a classmate claims: A negative discriminant means the equation has no solution. Explain to them what a negative discriminant really says
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the trap - A negative discriminant means the equation has no solution. The fix is: No real roots is not no solution: the equation still has two complex roots.

slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
bullets: On your own: state the discriminant of x^2 + 1 = 0 and what it says about the roots
Watch out for the trap one last time: A negative discriminant means the equation has no solution. Say what the roots of x^2 + 1 = 0 actually are
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - A negative discriminant means the equation has no solution. - and the fix: No real roots is not no solution: the equation still has two complex roots. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who still reads no real roots as no solution.
